articles.title: NBI subpoenas ‘Machong Chismisan’ hosts over ‘walang kwenta’ jab at Josh Aquino
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation has subpoenaed the five hosts of the podcast “Machong Chismisan” over an episode in which one of them called Kris Aquino’s eldest son, Josh, who…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 4:23pm
In a referral sent to the Department of Justice (DOJ), the NBI recommended charges against 12 officials of the DPWH-Davao district engineering office and private firm Genesis88 Construction Inc.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation has subpoenaed the five hosts of the podcast “Machong Chismisan” over an episode in which one of them called Kris Aquino’s eldest son, Josh, who is on the autism spectrum, “walang kwenta (useless).”

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said in an ambush interview on Friday, October 16, that the hosts must appear before the bureau’s Cybercrime Division at 2 p.m. on October 20. They could be charged with violating the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability and with cyber libel, he said.
Two of the "principal hosts" who made the utterances have received their subpoena, Matibag confirmed.
While the podcast hosts have issued a public apology, Matibag said this is not enough to shield them from potential criminal liability.
The podcast has since taken down the episode.
The remark was made in an October 5 episode titled “Ang Pagbabalik ni Kris Aquino," where host "Tito P" quipped that, compared to his younger brother: "Si Josh, walang kuwenta eh.”
The clips have since spread online, which triggered a wave of backlash against the hosts, including parents of children on the spectrum decrying the offensive remarks.
The hosts in their apology said their conduct was “inexcusable, deeply insensitive, and hurtful.”
The Pod Network has since terminated its contract with the podcast and pulled the show from its network.

Republic Act 7277, as amended by RA 9442, bans the public ridicule of persons with disabilities, defined as mocking or making fun of them, in writing, words or action, because of their impairment. A first offense carries a fine of P50,000 to P100,000, six months to two years in prison, or both.
The Autism Society Philippines has condemned the episode and reminded content creators that a person’s disability should not be fodder for jokes.
"As a community, we must not give our precious time to watching creators and listening to podcasts not capable of basic respect," it said.
"Disability is not a punchline. Freedom of expression must never come at the expense of the rights and humanity of persons with disabilities," it added.

articles.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
articles.summary: Sources say leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed

blocks.text: SETTING UP STARLINK. Servicemen of the 68th Oleksa Dovbush Separate Jaeger Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine set up Starlink satellite internet system, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, near the frontline town of Pokrovsk in Donetsk region, Ukraine on April 10, 2025.
Inna Varenytsia/Reuters
Sources say leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed

items: The White House is said to have ordered a slowdown of the SpaceX Starshield service used by Ukraine for military communications, impacting drone operations, according to sources.
Ukrainian officials reported that military-grade Starlink receptors faced issues when mounted on fast-moving objects, complicating strike missions against Russian forces.
Relations between the US and Ukraine have deteriorated, with tensions arising over Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and a recent US diesel deal with Russia.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.

The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday, October 15, that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph).

The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.

Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.

Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks.

That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to ​US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.

In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak.” Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy’s ouster.

Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.

The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office, Reuters reported in 2024. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU’s von der Leyen pledges to ‘not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war’ as leaders discuss Ukraine – Europe live
articles.summary:
European leaders are meeting in Brussels amid worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv

Irish PM Micheál Martin got asked about Ukraine on his arrival, too.

He…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoSituation in Ukraine 'really grave' and talks with US are 'very difficult,' EU foreign policy chief warns
9m agoIrish PM calls for 'a European response' to Ukraine's needs and outreach to the US
19m agoMorning opening: EU leaders meet to discuss Ukraine
19m ago'This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,' Costa says
19m ago'We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,' EU's von der Leyen says
19m agoZelenskyy thanks for support from 'real leaders' as he stresses need to prepare for winter
19m agoIf Europe wants to eat croissants, drink coffee and not think about threats - support Ukraine, Latvian PM says

blocks.text: Situation in Ukraine 'really grave' and talks with US are 'very difficult,' EU foreign policy chief warns
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warns on arrival that the situation in Ukraine is “really grave” with “no signs from Russia that they want to stop this war or into any sort of truce or peace.”

blocks.caption: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas speaks to the press as she arrives to attend an EU summit in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We need to support Ukraine, also to get through the winter, because winter is going to be harsh,” she warns. “And that’s why we really need to help Ukrainians to survive, to defend their country.”
Kallas says she expects the issue of frozen Russian assets to be raised again today.
She says “we have agreed that we will not return the frozen assets, unless Russia pays reparations for Ukraine.”
She says the EU is “trying to convince also our American partners” that more pressure needs to be put on Moscow.
“But you can see that with our American allies, it’s very difficult at the moment.”
Irish PM calls for 'a European response' to Ukraine's needs and outreach to the US
Irish PM Micheál Martin got asked about Ukraine on his arrival, too.

blocks.caption: Ireland’s prime minister Micheál Martin speaks with the media as he arrives for the EU summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Omar Havana/AP

blocks.text: He said “the very severe pressure that Ukraine is under needs a European response,” with the opening of the accession clusters, and the deploying of the EU’s €90bn loan to Ukraine as soon as possible.
He also says there needs to be a “clearer landscape” on what the EU can offer Ukraine in medium term, “whether it’s immobilised assets or other mechanisms.”
“I am conscious on the last occasion, we strongly supported the issue of the seizure, the seized assets and whether they could be deployed. But that came to nought in the end.”
He says Europe needs to “maintain the pressure on Russia.”

But he also notes that he wants to see “a continuing outreach from Europe to the United States,” making representations that “as far as Europe is concerned, Russia has been the aggressor from the beginning.”

“What is happening now is, really, without any sort of regard for innocent civilian life, Russia is simply bombing civilian infrastructure, and endeavouring to kill as many people as possible in Ukraine and to put as much pressure as possible on the civilian population in Ukraine to try and force a Ukrainian climbdown. The stakes are high and the situation is of considerable concern.”
If Europe wants to eat croissants, drink coffee and not think about threats - support Ukraine, Latvian PM says
Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs drops an early quote of the day contender, as he explains the stakes on Ukraine in direct and practical terms:

“It is a super important moment because, well, if we want comfort in Europe and [be able to] eat croissant, drink coffee in the morning, and don’t think about the threats, then we have to support Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs addresses the media in Brussels. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He says Russia “was pulled out from under the water” by Trump’s war in Iran and the crisis in the strait of Hormuz, which increased its oil revenues, “and that is not helping.”
“Ukraine needs financial support and military support in order to have to go through this harsh winter … ahead of us.”
Zelenskyy thanks for support from 'real leaders' as he stresses need to prepare for winter
In what definitely feels like a swipe at some other leaders (*waves across the ocean*), Zelenskyy begins his remarks by saying he is happy to have “huge support” from “leaders, real leaders.”

blocks.caption: Zelenskyy arriving for today’s EU summit Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He says Ukraine wants the war to end as soon as possible, but sees “no signals from the Russian side that they are ready to end this war.”
“That’s why we have to prepare for the winter,” both on energy and defence, he says.
'We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,' EU's von der Leyen says
Commission president von der Leyen also delivers a pretty unequivocal message, as she blames Russia for violating Donald Trump’s energy ceasefire and says Moscow “escalated” its attacks instead.

blocks.caption: Costa, Zelenskyy and von der Leyen arriving for today’s European Council. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: She makes it clear that the EU will not offer Russia any concessions, despite pressure from the US.
“One thing is absolutely clear: we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”
She says the talks today will also focus on defining Ukraine’s path to the European Union by opening two further “negotiating clusters” as they are known before the end of the year.
The leaders will also discuss how to support Ukraine during the winter.
'This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,' Costa says
Arriving with Zelenskyy and von der Leyen, Costa is very clear in his message on Ukraine as he declares the EU’s support to Ukraine “remains as strong as ever.”

blocks.caption: Costa, Zelenskyy and von der Leyen briefing journalists ahead of today’s meeting. Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP

blocks.text: In what feels like a targeted message to Ukraine, Russia, but also the US, he says:
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions.”
He adds “this is essential to bring Russia to accept a real ceasefire, to bring Russia to the table of negotiations and to stop this war.”
Costa also signals his intention to move on the accession prospects for Ukraine, saying:
“You can count on us not only to support you in war, but most important for your future as a member of the European Union.”
Morning opening: EU leaders meet to discuss Ukraine

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
EU leaders and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy are meeting today in Brussels to discuss the latest in Russia’s war against Ukraine amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington.

blocks.caption: Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives to attend a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Zelenskyy is expected to arrive any moment now, alongside European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa.
Overnight Ukraine was once again affected by Russian attacks, which killed at least three in the eastern city of Kharkiv. 370,000 people were left without power in the Volyn region bordering Poland.

Today’s talks come at a critical moment as Ukraine increasingly struggles with repelling Russian air attacks as a result of acute shortages of interceptor missiles, with Zelenskyy also involved in a very public series of disagreements with Donald Trump at White House.

The EU leaders will discuss what the bloc can do to support Ukraine during the upcoming winter and beyond and whether any substantial progress can be made on the key issue of its plans to join the European Union.
Separately, the leaders will also talk about migration and foreign policy more broadly.
I will bring you all the key updates here.
It’s Friday, 16 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals
articles.summary:
Regulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bust

Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers…

blocks.text: Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter.

Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices that caused more than 30 energy companies to go bust.

“We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility.
“In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.”

Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates.

“When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said.

When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He later posted an apology for his “emotional rant” on the social media platform X.
Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday: “It doesn’t sound a big deal, but it could be, it ain’t good for consumers and I don’t want it to slip under the radar.
“In a nutshell, it means if wholesale energy prices drop sharply, the cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits.”
Ofgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”.
after newsletter promotion
The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements.

“The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.”
Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month.
About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period.

Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872.
The chancellor, John Healey, is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.

articles.title: Wildfire kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
articles.summary: The latest victims of Indonesia's wildfires were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames, authorities said. Meanwhile, the toxic haze from the fires has spread to Indonesia's neighbors.

image.caption: Indonesia has been battling a months-long crisis of wildfiresImage: Abriansyah Liberto/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least four people have died and two others suffered severe burns while battling wildfires in a national park on Indonesia's main island, officials said on Friday.

They were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, a Forestry Ministry statement said, as the country's worst wildfires in a decade swept through the area.
The southeast Asian country has been battling a months-long crisis of blazes and toxic smoke, forcing schools to shut down and causing a surge in respiratory complaints in the region.

The victims were part of a 12-member firefighting team consisting of national park personnel, members of the community fire brigade, and local volunteers, said East Java police spokesperson Jules Abraham Abast.

"This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation," the ministry statement said, adding there had been a jump in hotspots detected by satellites as areas of unusually high temperatures. Not all hotspots necessarily translate into individual fires.

By Thursday evening, the number of hotspots in Indonesia stood at 799 , up from 372 a day earlier. The forest and land fires have worsened this year as weather phenomenon El Nino prolonged the dry season.
Communities fight back against fires in Indonesian Borneo
Toxic haze spreads across southeast Asia
The smoke from Indonesia's wildfires are causing a health crisis in neighboring southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Malaysia on Friday ordered hundreds of schools to close down due to deteriorating air quality.
Singapore, meanwhile, topped IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta sixth.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan rejected calls from some lawmakers to seek compensation from Indonesia, saying the crisis should be addressed through diplomatic engagement and established mechanisms.
He said Malaysia was coordinating assistance for Indonesia and would push for stronger regional cooperation on haze management.

blocks.caption: Toxic smoke from Indonesia's fires have enveloped much of MalaysiaImage: Arif Kartono/AFP

blocks.text: Singapore probing companies linked to fires

Singapore also called for closer cooperation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities were investigating companies allegedly linked to Indonesian forest and land fires that have worsened the haze.
"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," he said.
Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014 after a bout of severe pollution.

The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore. That said, legal experts cautioned that pursuing companies under the law will be challenging.

articles.title: No kids, no apologies: Why Filipino women are opting out of motherhood
articles.summary: An expert says the 'era of high fertility' that drove the country to overpopulation is over

blocks.text: First of two parts
Rubie Montejo was 24 years old and financially struggling as a call center agent when she first considered not having children.

“I was questioning a lot of my decisions and what direction to take with my career,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino. “And then, I thought to myself, I don't think I wanna involve another human being in this life when I have so many questions and confusion myself.”
She eventually told her mother about her decision and was met with unexpected support. However, things were different outside her home in the province.
Her neighbors voiced familiar warnings — cautioning Montejo that she would face regret, solitude, and lack of support from her would-have-been children in her old age.

“[Not having children] wasn't that normal before, especially if you grew up in the province as I did. Women were expected to, you know, marry at a certain age and then bear children after or before their 30s,” Montejo recalled.
But with her mother backing her choice, she gradually gained confidence. Now a 33-year-old, single, social media strategist, Montejo has fully embraced a child-free lifestyle.
“I could imagine [then] that it would be so much more difficult if a child were involved [in my life],” she said.
32-year-old Bea (not her real name) decided to have one child with her husband of three years and plans to stop there, despite relatives urging them to have one more so the child feels less lonely.

She explained that restructuring their existing savings would be a hassle if they had a second child. “It brings more happiness to be able to provide the comfortable life you can give your child,” Bea said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Although the Philippines remains within the working-age demographic range, its population has begun to resemble those of Asian neighbors such as Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, which are already aging.

Compared to these countries, the Philippines remains in transition. The Commission on Population and Development (CPD) expects the country to become an aging society by 2028, when Filipinos aged 65 and above reach 7% of the population.
The World Health Organization classifies a country as an “aging society” when the proportion of older people reaches this threshold.
Jose Ramon Albert, senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute of Development Studies (PIDS), said this new pattern is gradually displacing the longstanding concern of overpopulation.

“Philippine population policy was built around one fear: that population growth would outrun the economy's capacity to feed, educate, and employ people. The [data] tells us that the era of high fertility is over,” he told Rappler.
Change in socioeconomic status

Myline Quiray, Information Management and Communications Division chief of CPD, enumerated changing marriage patterns, increasing contraceptive use, declining number of desired children, and child health and survival as some of the top reasons for the trend.
However, she pointed to women’s socioeconomic status as the main driver.
“They're employed, they're educated — so the delay in fertility is happening,” she said.
Albert noted that as women have begun to outperform men in schools and stepped into diverse workforce roles, marriage and parenthood may become lower priorities for them.
Jireh Ramos, a 29-year-old law student who has been married for five years, opted for a child-free lifestyle to focus on higher education.
“I'm very intentional with the life I'm building right now. I have a career, I have law school, I have relationships, and I have a lot of things I want to experience in my life,” she said.

Ramos also feels content with their current routine at home: she studies for hours in a separate work room from her husband’s, shoots videos as a content creator on TikTok with 61,000 followers, takes breaks, and catches up with her husband at the end of the day.
Besides the need to focus on their own economic well-being, women also face pressure from rising household living costs, said Albert.

“Can you really blame people for deciding against having children or maybe deciding just to have one child instead of, like, three — when everything is getting more expensive while [salaries] in the Philippines do not keep up with inflation?” said Montejo.
Ramos also echoed the sentiment about costs and said, “Kids, in this economy, right? It’s perfectly valid. It really is expensive [to raise a child].”
Evolving marriage patterns, social media influence
The Philippines also saw a shifting pattern in marriage — or rather, a decreasing need for it.
In the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA) 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey, 42.7% of women aged 15-49 and in childbearing age have never married.

Albert noted that family formation itself has changed — couples now delay marriage, do not marry at all, or cohabit instead. “For many women, marriage is no longer an economic necessity, and childbearing is a choice weighed against other goals,” he said.
In 2020, common-law or live-in marital arrangements among households rose to 14.7% in 2020 from 9.2% in 2015.

As more opportunities open for women, Albert added that entering into marriage could also become less appealing without a “legal exit” such as divorce, so women would rather explore other forms of relationships.
Social media has also broadened exposure to alternative life paths centered on education, career, travel, or other forms of family formation through influencers.

Like Ramos, Montejo also does content on TikTok and openly discusses her childfree lifestyle. In one reel, she talked about the risk of passing down health conditions to children as a valid reason not to have kids.
On the other side of it, she pointed out that online platforms also harbor negative perspectives. She pointed to parents who "openly talk about how they wish they didn't have children."
“You see people talk about it openly like, ‘oh, this is the worst decision I've ever made in my life,’ and that's gonna influence you for sure… we didn't have that before,” she added.
Gaps remain
While the national fertility rate dropped to an all-time low, regional data still paint a different picture.
CPD’s Quiray admitted gaps in expanding education, family planning, and contraceptive use in the country’s poorer households and far-flung areas as possible explanations for the disconnect.
Minimum wage still varies per region, with Metro Manila having a nominal minimum wage of P695 while BARMM, Caraga, Bicol Region, and others are still at the P400 mark as of March 2026.
Experts noted that wage disparities make it more difficult for families in lower-income regions to afford raising children compared to reduction in highly-urbanized areas.

Albert stressed that empowering women in these areas to make informed family planning decisions requires expanding their access to healthcare, education, and jobs. “Invest early and where the children are,” Albert said.
Investing in women's capabilities
A falling fertility rate is not necessarily a bad thing, said the PIDS fellow, as it proves that the Philippines has successfully curbed overpopulation and is taking bold steps for women in society.
Instead of mitigating the decline, Quiray said the CPD is focusing on further increasing women’s capabilities.
“More than the human numbers, it's really the quality of life that matters… We cannot dictate or mandate Filipinos to have children or not to have children,” she said.

The CPD, under the current Philippine Population and Development Plan of Action, listed eight multisectoral objectives, including empowering women in the workforce, promoting healthy aging, responsible parenthood, and others.
When presented with more paths in life, Montejo and Ramos said women are freer to choose a lifestyle that suits them, whether or not with a child.

For Bea, motherhood does not dictate the limits of her potential. “Women today have so many choices regarding what they want to do, aside from being a mother.” (To be concluded) – with reports from Jake Gomez / Rappler.com

articles.title: Jenrick claims Farage has done more to stand against racism than ‘almost anybody’
articles.summary:
Reform MP defends leader after ITV footage shows official warning Farage he is ‘protecting’ candidate over racist David Lammy comments

The Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick sought to defend the…

blocks.text: The Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick sought to defend the party against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage had “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right.”

The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks against the former Labour deputy prime minister, David Lammy.

The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views.
In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy.
Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.

blocks.caption: Sarah Pochin is also seen in the ITV film saying Reform officials ‘are so fucking chauvinistic’ and that ‘they just exclude you if you are a woman’. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

blocks.text: Defending Farage and the party from the latest revelations on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, said: “(Farage) is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime.
“And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was his ultimate objective.”

Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.

However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Further footage released on Thursday shows Farage himself discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.

The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.

However, while Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.

In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.
“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”

To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”

On the Today programme, Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.”

He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

articles.title: Former student says someone hid a webcam in her Royal Military College dorm. No one was ever charged
articles.summary: A former student at the Royal Military College of Canada says she found a web camera hidden in her dorm room in October 2018. The Canadian Forces National Investigation Service investigated but no…

image.caption: Kelly Stewart says she left the Royal Military College of Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces because her mental health suffered greatly after discovering a webcam hidden in her dorm room without her consent. (Grant Linton/CBC News)

blocks.text: Kelly Stewart was plugging in her phone in her dorm room, planning to let it charge while she was in class at the Royal Military College of Canada (RMC), when she found a cord she didn't recognize — one she would later trace to a web camera hidden inside the heater in her wall.
"My whole body just went completely cold," she said during a recent interview at her home in Kingston, N.S.

Documents obtained by Stewart through Access to Information legislation, and shared with CBC News, show the Canadian Forces Military Police launched an investigation into voyeurism and breaking and entering offences on Oct. 31, 2018 — the same day Stewart discovered the webcam in her Kingston, Ont., dorm room and reported it to her superiors.

The following day, the National Investigation Service — a specialized unit that investigates serious matters — took over her case. According to the documents, no charges were ever laid due to insufficient evidence.

Eight years after the alarming discovery — and five years after a firestorm of sexual misconduct allegations in the Canadian Armed Forces prompted a federal review — Stewart is sharing her story publicly for the first time, emboldened by the support for a woman who alleges she was gang raped at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.
Stewart posted on social media on Oct. 3, writing that recent events out of Cornell had brought back painful memories.
"For 8 years I have carried the weight of other people's disgusting actions, failures and systemic sexism. I owe it to my 20-year-old self to pass that weight off to the men who failed."
Woman describes the moment she discovered the hidden webcam
Stewart files official complaint

Stewart, now 28, believes the investigation into her case was flawed, and though she believes the webcam was put in her room by another student, she says her superiors didn't support her, told her to "toughen up" and suggested her career could be affected by accessing mental health support.

She says her health suffered so much that she ultimately requested a voluntary release, which was granted in September 2019 on compassionate grounds, meaning she was not required to reimburse the government for the cost of her schooling.

In her social media post, Stewart named four people: her former superiors and a military police investigator. CBC News is choosing not to name them as there is no suggestion of any legal wrongdoing on their part.

The Department of National Defence (DND) has confirmed to CBC News that two of the four individuals have since retired. DND declined an interview, but in a statement said it is aware of claims, but for privacy and legal reasons it doesn't comment on matters involving identifiable individuals.
Stewart also filed a formal complaint on May 11, 2025, about the investigating officer. The Military Police Complaints Commission confirmed to CBC News that the complaint is being processed.

items: Q&A: Rear Admiral Angus Topshee addresses 'moment of reckoning' over sexual misconduct in Armed Forces

blocks.text: The 2018 RMC investigation
The 335-page military police report is heavily redacted but contains photos of the webcam, handwritten police notes and officer activity logs that shed some light on the investigation.

Stewart said she initially thought the investigation would reach a successful conclusion quickly. She felt her immediate, lower-level superiors took her seriously and there was a physical piece of evidence, the camera.
"I found myself a year later with nothing having been actioned," she said.
The documents show it took a month to access surveillance footage from the hallway outside Stewart's room, and that there was some confusion around whether an officer had even requested it.
Stewart said it took more than four months for the police to seize the suspect's laptop, which she said she witnessed herself. She believes it was the first time his laptop was taken.
Investigative photos that show the inside of Stewart’s dorm room at the RMC. Stewart says she found the webcam in the heater. (Canadian Forces National Investigation Service)
The documents show the investigation was formally closed on Aug 14, 2020 because it did not yield enough information to substantiate the elements of the offence.
The documents list one "person of interest." All the information about them is redacted.

items: The military's sexual misconduct crisis is turning into a national security problem, say experts

blocks.text: Stewart said around three months after she discovered the webcam, and after she had moved back into her dorm, a staff member at the college told her that her superiors knew who the suspect was and that he was living a few doors down from her. She said the staff member told her he had been told not to give her this information.
Having to continue living alongside the man she believed violated her was incredibly difficult, she said.
She said she repeatedly asked her superiors to move the suspect to another building but was told it was not possible — that she could move instead. She felt that was unfair.
Rare look at how Canadian Forces investigates sexual assault allegations
Stewart said she quit going to class, was afraid to go to the dining hall for fear of running into the suspect and lost a lot of weight.
She said a superior told her: "If you want a career in the military, you'll have to get used to being uncomfortable and not getting along with everybody."
Stewart's release records, which she provided to CBC News, state she performed well in all aspects at the college, up until her last semester, when she failed three courses.
Her release records state she was a victim of harmful and inappropriate sexual behaviour and that her release was directly related to that incident.
Sexual harassment not uncommon: former RMC student
CBC News has spoken with a male friend of Stewart's, who lived in the same dorm.
CBC News is withholding his name because he remains a serving member of the military and fears disciplinary repercussions that could affect his career progression.
He said he believes it was possible for RMC to move the suspect to another building to make things easier for Stewart.
"I just don't think they were thinking hard enough because they could have just moved a handful of people into different positions at the beginning of the next year."
He also said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there.
"I don't think I know a single one that didn't have something happen."
A friend of Stewart's said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

During her interview with CBC News, Stewart also disclosed that she had previously been sexually assaulted while she was a student at the French military college in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Que., before transferring to RMC.
She said she did not include that incident in her social media post because she did not report it. "At the end of the day, nobody failed me because I didn't do anything about it."
A 2023 survey of women attending Canadian military colleges, administered by the colleges, found that five per cent of women canvassed said they were sexually attacked during the previous 12 months.
Everyone deserves 'dignity and respect,' DND says
DND declined an interview, but called Stewart's assault allegations "very concerning," in a statement, stressing there is no time limit for making a report.
"Every Defence Team member has the right to serve in an environment where they are safe and treated with dignity and respect," the statement reads. "We know this standard has not always been met."

The statement goes on to say that in recent years DND and the CAF have taken steps to strengthen support for those affected by sexual misconduct, improve how incidents are reported, reinforce leadership accountability and create a safer culture.
On June 18, the Military Justice System Modernization Act received Royal Assent.

The new law means cases of sexual misconduct in the military will be transferred to the civilian justice system. It includes prohibiting military police from investigating voyeurism. There will be a mandatory external review in three years to determine whether the law should be repealed.
Anand issues apology to victims of sexual assault in Canadian Armed Forces
Only the passage of time will tell whether there has been meaningful change, said Megan MacKenzie, an expert in gender and the military at Simon Fraser University in B.C.
"We definitely have seen a commitment from many leaders, from many senior people to make changes," she said.
"Whether that is executed on a day-to-day basis for individual leaders and the people that they are responsible for, it's hard to know."
Stewart said she has been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder and complex post traumatic stress as a result of her experience.
She wants the higher chain of command to know her story.
"I want the colonels, the generals to hear this," she said. "I want them to wake up in the morning and go, 'What can I do differently to protect my subordinates?'"

items: New law to strip Canada's military of power to handle sexual assault cases

articles.title: Trudeau government advised it would be expected to carry out ICC arrest warrants, including for Netanyahu
articles.summary: An internal memo told Justin Trudeau's government that it was expected to pursue the arrests of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his then defence minister and Hamas leaders if the…

image.caption: Palestinians inspect the wreckage of a car after it was hit by an Israeli strike in Gaza City on Tuesday. The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in 2024 related to the war, including for crimes against humanity allegedly committed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (Jehad

blocks.text: Politics·New

An internal memo told Justin Trudeau's government that it was expected to pursue the arrests of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his then defence minister and Hamas leaders if the International Criminal Court were to issue the warrants being prepared by one of its prosecutors.
Adviser wrote in June 2024 that Canada has international obligations to ICC

Trudeau and his successor Mark Carney both later said they would act on the warrants. But the document — dated months before the warrants were ultimately issued — offers a rare glimpse at internal advice the government received from a non-partisan source.

"The International Criminal Court is a designated extradition partner under Canada's Extradition Act," Trudeau's national security adviser at the time, Nathalie Drouin, wrote in a memo dated June 10, 2024.
"Upon a request to co-operate, should one ever be received, Canada would be expected to seek an arrest warrant in a Canadian court," wrote Drouin, who is now Canada's ambassador to France.
CBC News asked the ICC and the federal government if Canada had received a request to co-operate related these warrants, but did not get an answer by deadline.
A protester holds a placard depicting an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Berlin on Oct. 10, 2026. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

The heavily redacted document, obtained by CBC News through an access to information request, is dated less than a month after ICC prosecutor Karim Khan sought applications for the arrests of Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, along with senior Hamas figures Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Mohammed Diab Ibrahim al-Masri.
Israel rejects the charges against Netanyahu and Gallant. The three Hamas leaders have all since been killed by the Israeli Defence Forces.

Immediately after the issuance of Khan's applications, Trudeau publicly said he was troubled by false equivalencies being drawn between Israel's democratically elected government and Hamas, which Canada lists as a terrorist organization.

Similarly, Trudeau's foreign affairs minister, Mélanie Joly, declined to answer journalists' questions about what the Canadian government would do if Netanyahu or Gallant ever came to Canada, calling such a scenario "hypothetical" as no warrants had yet been issued.

"The ICC may request that Canada, as a state party to the Rome Statute, co-operate in the provisional arrest or (if the subject is on the way or in Canada) in the arrest and surrender of that person," Drouin wrote.

Canada's Ambassador to France Nathalie Drouin speaks to reporters during the G7 summit in June. In her previous role, Drouin wrote a memo stating Canada has obligations to the International Criminal Court to enforce arrest warrants. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
"For example, Canada has received a request for provisional arrest following the issuance of a warrant against [Russian] President [Vladimir] Putin."

While the ICC issued its arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023, over a year after Canada prohibited Russian planes from entering its airspace, it is unclear in the memo when that provisional arrest request was received by Canada. CBC News requested more details from Global Affairs Canada but did not receive them by deadline.
The unredacted portions of the memo do not make clear whether Drouin's advice also applied to Canadian airspace.

Once the ICC warrants related to the war in Gaza were issued in November 2024, Trudeau said Canada would "abide by all the regulations and rulings of the international courts, this is just who we are as Canadians."
Joly reiterated Trudeau's stance, though neither explicitly used the word arrest nor named any individuals in their answers.

items: Canada, allies say they 'deeply regret' Palestinian elections being postponed
Trump wants to dismantle the ICC. These jurists want Canada to intervene

blocks.text: Carney has been slightly more explicit, saying "yes" in an interview with Bloomberg in October 2025, when he was asked about whether he would arrest Netanyahu should the latter enter Canada.
Netanyahu's government airplane, the Wing of Zion, has flown over Canadian airspace a number of times since the warrants were issued, with the federal government declining to turn the flights away.

On the latest occasion, during the Israeli prime minister's visit to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada said "authorization to pass through Canadian airspace should not be interpreted as an endorsement of the policies or actions of any particular government," adding that overflight request was related "to the United Nations General Assembly, a critical forum for diplomatic engagement."

Whether or not flying over sovereign airspace would require state parties to the Rome Statute to enforce ICC arrest warrants is a matter of debate. France has said its ICC treaty obligations do not extend to its airspace, while some international law experts argue that Canada and others failing to do so weakens the court.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Raffy Boudjikanian is a senior reporter with the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. He has also worked in Edmonton, Calgary and Montreal for the public broadcaster.
With files from Evan Dyer

articles.title: New Sense and Sensibility movie delves deep into the sisterly bond at the heart of Austen's classic
articles.summary: The new Sense and Sensibility adaptation brings Elinor and Marianne Dashwood’s bond to the foreground, using its natural landscapes and grounded style to give Jane Austen’s classic story a fresh…

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The new Sense and Sensibility adaptation brings Elinor and Marianne Dashwood’s bond to the foreground, using its natural landscapes and grounded style to give Jane Austen’s classic story a fresh perspective.
Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's classic
The sisterhood at the heart of Sense and Sensibility

It is the eternal question of the prestige drama. Do we really need another period piece? Do we really need another Jane Austen adaptation? More specifically, do we need another version of Sense and Sensibility?

For audiences familiar with director Ang Lee's 1995 Sense and Sensibility, the question might feel pointed. All of Austen's works have been adapted for the screen, and Sense and Sensibility alone has had at least five earlier adaptations.

Now comes director Georgia Oakley's Sense and Sensibility, which hits theatres Oct. 16. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and Esmé Creed-Miles as her sister, Marianne, and written by Diana Reid, this version doesn't try to out-romance the 1995 film.
Instead, it delves deeper into their sisterly bond and the financial insecurity that limits their choices.
A new lens on the Dashwood sisters

After their father's death, the Dashwood estate passes to their half-brother, leaving the women with limited financial security and forcing them to move to a more modest home. In Austen's time, women's prospects depended heavily on the goodwill of male relatives or the security of marriage, making this sudden loss of status and stability especially precarious.
The film's visual world moves with them: away from the controlled elegance of the drawing room and out into the open countryside, amid weather, mud and unkempt fields.
They garden, go on long walks, run on the beach and wade through ponds. While Elinor finds peace in sketching and skipping rocks, Marianne is often seen lying in fields, watching the clouds.
Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood, left, and Daisy Edgar-Jones as her older sister Elinor sort through their belongings as they prepare to leave their family home. (Universal Pictures)
That rougher setting makes their vulnerability physical as well as financial — and brings their shared experience into view.

Elinor's restraint can conceal how deeply she feels and Marianne's openness leaves her more exposed to heartbreak. Throughout the film, circumstances bring each of them to see the other's perspective.
'The sisters are the constant'
"They really wanted to centralize the love story as being the two girls," Edgar-Jones said of Oakley and Reid's approach.
She also told CBC News that working with her longtime friend Creed-Miles felt effortless.

items: Persuasion modernizes Jane Austen for a new generation — but does it lack sense and sensibility?

blocks.text: "I had an idea of who I thought Elinor was, but it wasn't until I really started acting those scenes with Esmé's Marianne that I really understood her," she said.
Creed-Miles says their friendship quickly helped them find a "familial, sisterly, best friend sort of energy." She says she "couldn't have gotten through the project" without Edgar-Jones's support.
Why Sense and Sensibility still resonates
The sisters are each other's confidantes, critics and support system.
Canadian author Natalie Jenner, whose novel, The Jane Austen Society, draws on Austen's work and life, sees that connection as one reason the book continues to resonate.

"If your family relationships are strong, you feel emboldened to take on anything," Jenner said. "The sisters are the constant. And that sense of constancy and a North Star is something that you can always go back to. I think that taps into a modern need for community and stability," she told CBC News.
A different kind of Brandon and Willoughby
Marianne’s love interests are John Willoughby, played by Frank Dillane, left, and Colonel Brandon, played by Herbert Nordrum. (Universal Pictures)
The new film's male characters offer a departure from the archetypes established in Ang Lee's 1995 adaptation.

In an interview with CBC News, Herbert Nordrum explains that he played Colonel Brandon as awkward and difficult to read, focusing on the character's internal struggle to express his feelings. This contrasts with Alan Rickman’s 1995 performance, which gave Brandon a sense of gravitas and a devotion to Marianne expressed through quiet, powerful gestures.

items: Why Jane Austen is as relevant as ever

blocks.text: In the 1995 adaptation, Greg Wise portrays Willoughby as a dashing romantic hero, making his betrayal all the more shocking. In the 2026 version, Frank Dillane told CBC News he wanted to emphasize Willoughby’s sweeter qualities — "his joy, his exuberance, his lust for life, poetry and romance" — while still letting his questionable actions speak for themselves. He aimed to portray him as a rounded young man who makes mistakes and falls in love.
He jokes that Willoughby's grand romantic gestures would now be called "love bombing," while his habit of ignoring Marianne's letters is the period-drama equivalent of "ghosting."

In Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon (Alan Rickman) carries Marianne Dashwood (Kate Winslet) through the rain after finding her gravely ill. (Sony Pictures Releasing)
What Austen means to audiences now
While Lee's film is lush and sweeping, Oakley's is quieter and more grounded. It doesn't try to replace the older version; it's asking what these stories can mean to audiences now.
Jenner says Austen's characters endure because they're trying to find happiness without losing themselves. "You've got to know what makes you happy," she told CBC News, "and stay true to that."

items: The everpresent influence of Jane Austen
70 facts you might not know about iconic British novelist Jane Austen

blocks.text: She introduced her own daughter to Austen's books and films when she was seven or eight. Jenner wanted her to meet characters who were "strong-spirited" and full of "intellect, brightness, vivacity, kindness, curiosity."
Jenner says she believes younger audiences are craving more naturalistic depictions — a shift she noticed through conversations with her daughter, now in her mid-20s.
Elinor (Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Creed-Miles) share a quiet moment in a field of tall grass. (Universal Pictures)

She says that coming out of the pandemic, there's been a longing for a return to nature and the simple warmth of picnics, books and blankets, which has seeped into the visual style of modern adaptations.

Jenner believes that Austen doesn't belong to one decade or one aesthetic. Her stories offer romance, but also friendship, family, community and the difficult work of figuring out what kind of life will make you happy.
The question of whether the world really needs another Sense and Sensibility remains.
Audiences may well find that it does, not because of a desire to surpass previous versions, but because Austen's story is timeless enough to invite a completely new interpretation.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: China’s ByteDance sets up AI safety team, launches global hiring drive
articles.summary: The hiring push comes as scrutiny of AI-agent safety grows in China and the US, especially as developers give them autonomy to access the Internet

blocks.text: BYTEDANCE. The Bytedance logo is seen in this illustration taken February 8, 2025.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The hiring push comes as scrutiny of AI-agent safety grows in China and the US, especially as developers give them autonomy to access the Internet

items: ByteDance's AI research unit Seed has launched a global recruitment drive for 10 researchers to focus on AI safety and alignment, marking a significant investment in this area.
The establishment of a dedicated safety and alignment team is a notable move among Chinese AI developers, coinciding with increasing scrutiny of AI safety in both China and the US.
Seed plans to provide substantial resources for the new team and aims to collaborate with universities and research institutions to enhance AI safety across various stages of model development.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Chinese tech giant ByteDance’s AI research unit Seed has created an Alignment & Preparedness team and launched a global drive to recruit 10 researchers, saying it will make a long-term investment in AI safety for its increasingly capable models.
The hiring push comes as scrutiny of AI-agent safety grows in China and the US, especially as developers give them autonomy to access the Internet.
AI alignment refers to efforts to ensure advanced AI systems act in line with human goals and safety requirements, particularly when carrying out complex, multi-step tasks.
ByteDance’s announcement is a rare public disclosure by a major Chinese AI developer of a dedicated effort focused on frontier-model safety, alignment and preparedness for emerging risks.
State-backed newspaper The Paper reported on Tuesday, October 13, that Seed was the first Chinese frontier AI lab to establish a standalone safety and alignment department.

The move also comes amid broader US-China discussions on AI guardrails, safety risks and channels for communicating about major AI-related incidents, even as the two countries compete for leadership in advanced AI.

As model capabilities improve, safety and alignment are no longer simply safeguards against risk but core capabilities that will determine whether models can be deployed at scale, Seed said in a recruitment post published on its official WeChat account on Wednesday.

Seed said it would provide the new team with computing capacity and research resources comparable to those available to frontier-model teams. The positions are based in Beijing, Shanghai, and San Jose, California.

Its research will include safety training across model-development stages, automated testing for vulnerabilities, tools to monitor and explain model behavior, AI-agent testing environments and preparations for emerging risks.
Seed said it would also seek independent testing and work with universities and research institutions, applying safety research across model training, evaluation and deployment. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskyy says ‘we’re done’ with Trump’s energy truce
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites but in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking…

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites but in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people

KYIV, Ukraine – Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, October 15, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticized Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Moscow.

By effectively walking away from Trump’s demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticizing the US leader, Zelenskyy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine’s latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia’s refinery throughput, helping supply the capital.
Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack had caused a fire at the refinery.
Russian President Vladimir Putin played down the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused “nothing particularly significant.”

After Trump’s surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets.
But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people.
Zelenskyy’s relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match.
Zelenskyy has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s patience had run out.
“The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper.
Zelenskyy also criticized what he saw as Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth.

“He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people,” the FT quoted him as saying. “Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong.”

In his comments to the FT, Zelenskyy also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine’s ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.

British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said on Thursday that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to “move forward in a collective spirit.”

“We need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression,” he said on Fox News.
Zelenskyy was due to attend a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air defenses.
In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote.

Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had “damn well better stop”.
Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington.
Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles.
Trump has denied withholding intelligence.

At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.

A source in Ukraine’s defense ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones.

Defense experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, showed that Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones.

Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia.

Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks,. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices.

In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine.

The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 11 Negros Occidental wind projects advance along bird migration route
articles.summary: Concerns regarding the projects' impact on bird migration routes are being addressed, and the developments align with the province's goal to transition to renewable energy and reduce reliance on…

blocks.text: Concerns regarding the projects' impact on bird migration routes are being addressed, and the developments align with the province's goal to transition to renewable energy and reduce reliance on fossil fuels

items: Eleven wind farm projects are being developed in Negros Occidental, with a combined capacity of 3,767 megawatts, scheduled for commissioning between 2027 and 2030.
The projects are located in various cities and municipalities along the coastline facing the Guimaras Strait, which is favorable for wind energy due to strong winds.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
NEGROS OCCIDENTAL Philippines – Eleven wind farm projects are moving forward in Negros Occidental, all facing the Guimaras Strait, a bird migration route.
The province’s coastline facing the strait is conducive to wind energy development because of its strong winds.
Eleven cities and municipalities in Negros Occidental are set to host the projects.
The cities are Cadiz, Silay, Victorias, Talisay, Bacolod, Bago and Kabankalan, while the municipalities are Manapla, E.B. Magalona, Pulupandan and Cauayan.
The projects, scheduled for commissioning and commercial operations between 2027 and 2030, have a combined capacity of 3,767 megawatts (MW).

William Carido of the Department of Energy (DOE) Visayas identified the project proponents during the “Be REeady” Caravan organized by the Provincial Energy Development Council (PEDC) in Himamaylan City on Wednesday, October 14, as the following:

items: Bago-Negros Energy Corporation
Envision Energy Philippines Corporation
Apolaki One Incorporated
Energy Development Corporation
Triconti Southwind Corporation
Freya Renewables
First Gen Visayas Energy Incorporated
Haraya Wind Energy Corporation

blocks.text: Carido said the 11 wind farms are currently classified as indicative projects but are expected to proceed, as their proponents could face penalties from the DOE if they fail to meet their commitments.
According to the DOE’s schedule, the 200-MW Cauayan Wind Project, developed by Envision Energy Philippines, is expected to be the province’s first wind farm to enter operation.
Commissioning is targeted for October 2027, with commercial operations scheduled for December 2027.

The next project is Bago-Negros Energy Corporation’s 300-MW wind farm in Bago City, covering phases 1 and 2. It is scheduled for commissioning in October 2028 and commercial operations in December of that year.
Bago City held a groundbreaking ceremony on June 10 for phase 1 of the project, which has a capacity of 150 MW.
Both the Cauayan and Bago projects are onshore wind farms.
The last project scheduled for development is Haraya Wind Energy’s 1,215-MW Haraya IV-Negros Wind Project, which is expected to begin commercial operations in May 2030.
The DOE has yet to identify a specific site within the province for the project.

Rafael Coscolluela, a former Negros Occidental governor who now serves as a provincial consultant on energy and environmental issues, said the 11 projects would comprise both onshore and offshore wind farms.
Offshore development poses significant challenges, he said.
The DOE has yet to determine which cities and municipalities will host the onshore and offshore projects.

Coscolluela said proponents would face lengthy procedures to secure an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and an environmental compliance certificate (ECC) from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources.

The DOE Visayas office said energy projects with capitalization of at least P3.5 billion may qualify for a Certificate of Energy Project of National Significance (CEPNS), which can help streamline and expedite permitting.

On concerns about the projects’ proximity to the Guimaras Strait bird migration route, Coscolluela said an initial agreement with proponents called for painting turbine blades in bright colors to make them more visible to birds.
Coscolluela welcomed the wind farm developments, noting that Negros Occidental was declared coal-free on March 6, 2019, when then-governor Alfredo Marañón Jr. signed Executive Order No. 19-08.
The order has not been repealed and remains in effect, he said.
“The only hurdle is, can Negros Occidental benefit from the power to be produced by wind farms?” Coscolluela said.
He said the province’s three distribution utilities could be encouraged to prioritize contracts with solar and wind power producers as their existing power supply agreements (PSAs) expire.
Wind farms would also contribute to the province’s goal of gradually shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy as part of its energy transition and decarbonization efforts, he said.
The national target is for renewable energy to account for 35% of the country’s energy mix by 2030, Coscolluela said.
“SecuRE Negros,” an energy program backed by PEDC, aims to contribute to that national goal, he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations
articles.summary:
David Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commission

  • Get our

blocks.text: Greens leader David Shoebridge has denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.

The Nine newspapers reported on Friday afternoon the existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.
Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.
In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.
“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.
“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”

Steele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.

The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.

Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service, which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.

The PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission.
Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.
The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.

A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”
Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.
“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.

“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”
