articles.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
articles.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.

blocks.text: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.

Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
They are part of a defiant French tradition.

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the ­biggest general strike in French ­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.

"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".

"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."

I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."

"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

articles.title: Lawyer urges Supreme Court to clarify ruling on senior discounts, promos
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 7:00am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should issue a clear elaboration on its ruling barring the application of a senior citizen discount after other promotional discounts have been applied, a senior citizen advocate said.

In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate and lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting senior citizen discounts.

According to the Supreme Court’s ruling released in a press briefer on October 14, senior citizens cannot stack their statutory 20% discount on top of existing promotional prices, reinforcing that elderly consumers must choose between the promotional price and the statutory 20% discount, whichever yields greater savings.

While the ruling acquitted a hotel executive in Bacolod City after finding that the guests had already received a 20% discount through a pre-negotiated group rate, Macalintal emphasized that the public briefer lacks critical legal distinctions.
Macalintal pointed out that the denial of the discount in the Bacolod hotel case stemmed specifically from a pre-negotiated group association rate rather than a standard commercial sales promotion.

Without explicit clarification from the justices, he warned that commercial establishments might improperly label regular transactions or self-run "house promos" as promotional offers to deny elderly customers their rightful 20% discount.

“This clarification is very crucial and imperative because establishments may have the impression that they can just conduct promos on their own or run house promos to deny a senior citizen their 20% discount,” Macalintal’s statement read.

“This distinction is vital. Without it, establishments might falsely label regular transactions as ‘promos’ to evade granting senior discounts, entirely defeating the protective intent of the law,” he added.

Addressing the legal mechanism behind promotional pricing, Macalintal stressed that under Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, any company intending to conduct a promotional campaign must first secure a permit from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) before launching the offer.

According to Macalintal, an establishment cannot legally invoke the non-concurrence or "double-discount" rule unless the promotion has prior approval from the DTI and is set for a specified timeframe.
“Clearly, an establishment conducting a promo without a DTI permit is still obligated to extend to a senior citizen the 20% discount over and above the unauthorized promo price,” Macalintal said.
Macalintal also pointed out that the prohibition against double-discounting does not strip senior citizens of their statutory value-added tax exemption.

He also urged the high court to clarify in its full written decision that senior citizens utilizing hotel services remain entitled to their 12% VAT exemption alongside their applicable price reduction.

articles.title: How did a P.E.I. cold case fall apart just before it was set to go to trial?
articles.summary: There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to…

blocks.text: Criminologist weighs in on Charlottetown police's handling of Byron Carr murder investigation

There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to go to trial.

The provincial Crown Attorney’s Office announced Tuesday that the charges against Todd Joseph Irving in connection with the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr were being withdrawn after it came to light that Charlottetown police had lost "extensive crucial evidence" in the case.

CBC News first learned about that missing evidence — which includes the knife found at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr — at a bail hearing in July. The Crown confirmed that’s when they first learned about it, too. But Charlottetown police later told CBC News they knew physical evidence was missing as far back as 2007 when the case was reopened.

items: Charges were dropped in a decades-old murder case. Now, there are calls for an independent review
Charlottetown police lost the evidence in a P.E.I. cold-case murder. How did it happen?

blocks.text: Interim Charlottetown police Chief Darren MacDougall believes police did tell the Crown at some point that some items were missing, but not the full picture of how much physical evidence or exactly which items were lost.
He acknowledges that information should have been provided to the Crown sooner.

"There was likely not enough transparency with regard to the evidence as it relates to the Crown and the investigators. So there was certainly a breakdown there. I think that the investigators clung to the hope that they would be able to interview some of the people involved in 1989 to determine where they might have put these exhibits," MacDougall said.
"It’s the responsibility of the police, for full disclosure, to move that disclosure to the Crown."

But MacDougall was quick to point out that the DNA evidence collected from the items wasn’t lost — that material was processed and stored appropriately. It was the items themselves, after they’d been processed and sent back to Charlottetown police, that were misplaced.
Calls mount for an investigation into how crucial evidence in P.E.I. murder case was lost
Michael Arntfield is a professor and criminologist at Western University who heads up the school’s cold case research group. He’s also a former police detective.

"It’s both unusual and unfortunate because this was a great solve using state-of-the art investigative genetic genealogy, IGG, to track down the still alleged or once alleged offender in a very infamous cold case," he said.

"However, it turned out to be sort of an exploding cigar in that once, sort of, the novelty of the solve subsided … the two key pieces of evidence seem to have disappeared, which sort of pulls the rug out from underneath the whole case."
'It contaminates the whole investigation'
Arntfield believes police were hoping the DNA evidence was incontrovertible. And police have said as much.
Todd Joseph Irving walked out of court on Tuesday a free man after the charges against him in connection with the death of Byron Carr were dropped. (CBC)

"With the evidence that we relied upon, and we had significant forensic DNA evidence, we believed the evidence met the threshold to believe that [Irving] committed the offense," MacDougall said in an interview with CBC News after the charges were dropped.
At the July bail hearing, police testified that Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.

His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind, according to police testimony.

The entirety of the missing evidence isn’t clear, but the Crown described it as "the overwhelming majority of the critical physical evidence," going on to say that included "key exhibits central to the prosecution."

items: Family of Byron Carr speaks out after murder charges in decades-old cold case withdrawn
Charges laid in decades-old P.E.I. cold case murder withdrawn after key evidence lost

blocks.text: With that, Arntfield said, the credibility of the Charlottetown Police Services is lost — along with whatever remaining evidence they had.

"It contaminates the whole investigation because a judge or jury or both … would be left wondering, 'OK, if they have slipshod record-keeping and no chain of custody for key exhibits, what else don’t we know? What else was overlooked? What other corners were cut?'" he said.

"This isn’t corruption, this isn’t malicious. What I think it is is they were fixated on solving this, they cut corners and ultimately at the end of the day they were motivated by getting an alleged killer off the streets and ensuring justice for the family decades later."
What happened to missing evidence in the Byron Carr murder case? Charlottetown's interim police chief explains
If police had been forthcoming with the Crown about what physical evidence they did — and didn’t — have in their possession, Arntfield said the outcome could have been much different.

"You would think in a case like this — a high-profile historical homicide using a state-of-the-art and still somewhat controversial technology, IGG — that, even just as a courtesy, some senior officer or the case manager might have notified the Crown that a complex, high-profile case is coming down the pipe, apprise them of the strengths and weaknesses of the case, what witnesses are still alive and locatable and exhibits are still intact," he said.

"There’s other things that could have been done based on what police knew in order to shore up those deficiencies.… I think they would have had probably more evidence to incentivize maybe a quick guilty plea, which is I’m almost certain what police were relying on here. They were expecting a quick guilty plea and none of this suspicious disappearance of evidence would have ever seen the light of day."
Police, Crown look through different lenses: MacDougall
In Ontario, Arntfield said, cold cases get what he calls a "concierge approach," where the Crown is brought in early to weigh in on the strength of the evidence.
MacDougall acknowledges that, in this case, investigators were perhaps weighing the strength of the evidence differently than a prosecutor might.

"Perhaps the Crown, who views this through a different lens — the weight that existed with the missing exhibits measured with the weight of the DNA evidence, the forensic DNA evidence that was very compelling, I would say — [the Crown], again viewing it through a different lens, they came to the conclusion that they were unable to provide the accused with a fair trial."
Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, says he would welcome an independent investigation. (Barry Acton/CBC)
While Arntfield called the outcome of this case a rare and regrettable snafu, he said it shouldn’t erode public confidence in police.

"The investigation was solid, there was a chokepoint along the way where something happened and I wouldn’t even call it a coverup, I would say they strategically omitted that information at the last minute," he said.
"The question will be: who made the determination to suppress this glaring deficiency and suspicious disappearance and proceed at great time and expense?"
There have been calls for an independent review of how the case was handled, which MacDougall said he would welcome.

It’s up to P.E.I.'s justice and public safety minister to call such an investigation. In a statement to CBC News, the department said it was communicating with Charlottetown police about the Byron Carr case, saying "government has various options to consider in terms of a review and scope, so a particular path is not set yet. It's still under discussion."
Why were all charges dropped in the P.E.I. cold-case murder of Byron Carr?

articles.title: Oregon school shooting: Gunman kills 3 students and teacher before being shot dead by community member
articles.summary: A 16-year-old gunman opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing three children and a teacher. Two others were wounded. A community member pursued and killed the suspected shooter,…

image.caption: A shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, has left multiple victims, police said Thursday.Image: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher and wounded two others in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday before a community member pursued and killed him, authorities said.
"The deceased at the scene include three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters. Another child and a teacher were injured and taken to a hospital.
The first 911 call came in around 1 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone carrying a long gun, Krantz said.
Additional 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. Officers arrived within minutes.
"Seconds later, we received word over the radio that the suspect in this incident was down," Miller said.
Students evacuated as police respond to shooting
Bend is a ​city of some ‌100,000 people in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

blocks.caption: Students were evacuated from the school and the buildings were cordoned offImage: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An updated post later said law enforcement was escorting students by bus to a separate location, where they could reunite with their families. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly children aged ⁠5 to ​11. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek thanked the community member who "heroically intervened to ​stop further loss of life."

"No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have ​to live through ‌this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to ‌cry privately," Kotek said.
US grapples with recurring mass shootings

The United States, where firearms are widely available, experiences frequent gun violence, with thousands of people killed each year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among high-income countries.

blocks.caption: Emergency personnel directed people away from the schoolImage: Rob Kerr/REUTERS

blocks.text: The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007. South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 365 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter.

articles.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate over post minimizing Holocaust
articles.summary: A B.C. Conservative candidate has been dropped after he was accused of posting offensive remarks on social media.

image.caption: Jordan McIntosh has been dropped as a B.C. Conservative candidate in Vancouver-Strathcona. (B.C. Conservative party website)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A B.C. Conservative candidate has been dropped after he was accused of posting offensive remarks on social media.
Jordan McIntosh dropped as the candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona
The party says Jordan McIntosh is no longer its candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona and that if elected, he will not sit in caucus.

The Conservatives announced his removal from the slate less than an hour after Callista Ryan, the NDP’s candidate for Vancouver-Quilchena, posted screenshots on social media platform X, showing what she said were McIntosh’s posts.
"Looks like Lorne Doerkson's candidate in Strathcona Jordan McIntosh thought he could use a nameless twitter account to say many awful, offensive things," Ryan said.
A post from an account linked to McIntosh repeated false claims that minimize aspects of the Holocaust.
The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs says they're glad the B.C. Conservatives acted quickly to remove McIntosh as a candidate.
Nico Slobinsky, the group's vice-president Pacific region, said on social media that the posts were "reprehensible and harmed our community by distorting the history of the Holocaust."
"Accountability matters for all seeking elected office," he said.
Ryan said the latest incident raises concerns about the Conservatives' vetting process.
"I see these comments as hateful, and that's something we absolutely have to call out and address."

McIntosh is a university student working toward a BA in geological engineering, according to his biography, which has since been removed from the party’s website. His LinkedIn page says he attends the University of Waterloo in Ontario.

A party spokesperson speaking on background says McIntosh was informed he was no longer a candidate shortly after Ryan's social media post. McIntosh is 18 years old and the party says it appears the posts were made when he was 15.
CBC News called a number listed as McIntosh's campaign number but it was not in service. It's unclear if McIntosh will run as an Independent.
The Vancouver-Strathcona riding was previously held by Joan Phillip, who died on Aug. 28.

items: B.C. Conservatives drop Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after offensive social media posts

blocks.text: Amanda Burrows, who has served as director for First United in the Downtown Eastside, is the NDP’s candidate in that riding. It’s considered one of the safest NDP seats in the province.
This is the second time the B.C. Conservatives have dropped a candidate over offensive social media posts.
Last week, the party fired Joachim Agou in light of social media posts targeting Palestinians and Pakistanis that came to light.
B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts
Doerkson has also faced calls from the Unified Muslim Associations of B.C. to drop Katy Merrifield as the party’s campaign director over anti-Islam posts.
Merrifield posted on X in June in response to a U.K. inquiry about child sexual exploitation: "F--k Islam. Defend Western civilization." The post was later removed.

items: B.C. Conservative campaign director under fire for anti-Islam posts

blocks.text: During Wednesday night's B.C. leaders' debate, Doerkson defended Merrifield, saying she is a sexual assault survivor who made the comments out of anger. Doerkson said she has since apologized and he will not remove her.
Doerkson hit back by accusing Eby of failing to stand up to antisemitism within the NDP, which led to the departure of former cabinet minister Selina Robinson.

items: Former cabinet minister Selina Robinson resigns from NDP caucus

blocks.text: The party did not make Doerkson available for an interview about McIntosh’s removal or the party's vetting process.
NOTE (Oct. 15, 2026): This story has been updated to remove misinformation contained in a social media post linked to Jordan McIntosh.

articles.title: How the $90M Lotto Max jackpot stacks up against other big Canadian lottery prizes
articles.summary: Friday's $90-million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada. We break down your odds of winning and how this jackpot compares to past prizes.

image.caption: A clerk at a gas station near Newcastle, Ont., hands a customer their Lotto Max ticket in October 2022. Thinking of getting in on the $90-million jackpot currently up for grabs in the Lotto Max? We break down your odds of winning Canada's largest lottery prize to date and compare it to past wins. (D

blocks.text: Canada·New
Friday's $90-million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada. We break down your odds of winning and how this jackpot compares to past prizes.
Friday's jackpot will be the largest prize in Canadian lottery history
Friday's $90 million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada — may the odds be ever in your favour.
(Even though, statistically, they're very much not.)
Draws take place every Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 p.m. ET. Tuesday's previously record-setting $85-million jackpot rolled over after no one claimed it, which allowed the prize pool to keep growing.
Lotto Max, a national lottery, announced in April that it was increasing its jackpot cap from $80 million to $90 million, but this is the first time it's actually happened.
So, what are the odds of winning? And how does this compare to past jackpots?
Let's break it down.
Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by two friends in London, Ont., last December. At the time, the men said they were still overcome with shock that they'd won. (OLG)
What are the odds of winning?
Don't quit your job in anticipation just yet.

The odds of winning the main jackpot are one in 33 million per $6 play, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG), the Crown agency that manages and conducts gaming and lottery operations across the province.
Let's put that into perspective.

You're almost exactly as likely to flip a coin 25 times in a row and have it land on "heads" each time — an extremely rare probability of one in 33.5 million, according to the scientifically developed coin flip probability calculator.
Meanwhile, the odds of being struck by lightning in Canada are less than one in a million, according to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.
And we're sorry to say that you're actually far more likely to be killed by an asteroid's impact on Earth on your way to buy the ticket than you are of winning the $90-million jackpot.
How does the $90M compare?
However, despite these odds, people do win the lottery. And the prizes keep growing.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by a pair of long-time friends in London, Ont., last December. They won the $80-million Lotto Max jackpot and the $403,285.40 second prize in the combination play option.
At the time, the men, identified only as Greg S. and Krys P., said they weren't sure how they would spend the money.

Before that, the top prize was claimed by a B.C. man who won the $80 million Lotto Max jackpot in May 2025. Justin Simporios of Surrey quit his job hours before the news conference where he claimed his cheque.

items: Pair of longtime friends in London, Ont., win over $80.4M in largest-ever lottery payout in Canada
Who won the lottery? Why you may never know the full name of some jackpot winners going forward

blocks.text: Lotto Max's first $80-million draw in September 2024, was split between two winning tickets sold in Ontario and Quebec. The first $70-million prize was in 2020, and the first $65-million draw was in 2019. (It was actually the second time the $65-million winner, a family in Montreal, had won the lottery).

The first Lotto Max draw for $60 million was in 2015, after the lottery changed the rules previously capping the jackpot at $50 million. Two years before that, however, a record-breaking $63.4 million Lotto 649 prize was split between four tickets.

Some may also recall 2005, when 17 oil and gas workers from Alberta split Canada's biggest jackpot to date, a whopping $54 million. Before that, the previous lottery record was $37.8 million, split between four tickets in a Super 7 draw in 2002.
Canada's first national lottery dates back to 1974, when nine women from Quebec City split the $1-million prize in a lottery held to raise money for the Montreal Olympics.

articles.title: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia didn't pass the bar exam
articles.summary: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president's chief spokeswoman.

image.caption: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is seen at Glacier Park International Airport in Kalispell, Mont., on Wednesday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president's chief spokeswoman.
Zacharia has faced scrutiny over her resume and legal background
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is defending her legal background, while acknowledging that she did not pass the bar exam.

In an interview with the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia said she was preparing to take the California bar exam at a time when she had just gotten married and was preparing to move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.
"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia said.
She said the results of the bar exam, which she did not pass, were "somewhat inconsequential" because she would not need to be a barred attorney while living in China.
Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny for calling herself a "lawyer," said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.

"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."
Zacharia said she will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House role.
Showed 'ample deference' to Trump
Zacharia also spoke to Human Events about her start to her new job as press secretary — including her truncated inaugural press briefing on Tuesday.

She said she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing and that the plan had always been to keep it short because U.S. President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.
New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live

"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Zacharia said. "So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."

The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed on Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said.
"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.
Trump called her about job

She also revealed details about how she secured the White House press secretary job. Zacharia stressed that she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, which became vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.

Zacharia, who was a communications adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, said she closely monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.

"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job. I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."
Zacharia says that U.S. President Donald Trump called about the press secretary position on Oct. 7. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Then on Oct. 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.
She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.

articles.title: Canada courting Indian business partnerships in race to seal trade deal
articles.summary: Canada’s largest trade mission to India in 30 years has netted about 30 commercial partnerships worth $300 million, according to International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu.

image.caption: The Team Canada trade mission to India took this 'family photo' in Mumbai, India, this week. The trade mission is the largest in 30 years. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

blocks.text: World
Canada’s largest trade mission to India in 30 years has netted about 30 commercial partnerships worth $300 million, according to International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu.
Canadian international trade minister touts $300 million in commercial partnerships
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 15, 2026 4:10 PM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago
"It’s a market we can’t ignore," Sidhu told CBC News in an interview in Mumbai this week.
Sidhu is leading a weeklong trade pitch in New Delhi, Mumbai and Bangaluru with a 300-member Team Canada to connect Canadian businesses and industry with Indian ventures.

It's the prelude to a significant trade pact, CEPA (Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement), which Canada is racing to conclude before mid-December, when India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada.
Canada is looking to bring down Indian tariffs, including on commodities such as pulses and potash.
International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu on Indian tariffs

The Team Canada mission reflects a significant shift in Canadian-Indian relations, which ruptured three years ago after Justin Trudeau's government said intelligence showed "credible allegations" linking Indian government agents to the fatal shooting of a Sikh separatist leader in B.C. India’s government called the claims "absurd," touching off political and diplomatic tensions. Canada expelled a diplomat, India followed suit.
The Canada-India reset over the past two years has been dramatic, says Harsh V. Pant, a strategic analyst and vice-president at ORF Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
Both sides have worked hard to ensure that the challenges — terrorism, law enforcement, cybersecurity and internal security — are being dealt with, says Pant.
"That's why perhaps one needs to be a bit more optimistic about the possibility of this [trade] dance going forward," he said.
Massive population, booming economy
India’s population of 1.4 billion and seven per cent economic growth rate is a big draw for business.
Team Canada delegates squeeze into a shop in Crawford Market in southern Mumbai to hear about what Canadian goods are imported and sold at this specialty store. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
During a visit to Mumbai’s hot and crowded Crawford Market, about two dozen Team Canada delegates sweated their way from stall to stall, looking at packaged goods and the ways they are sold.

Agri-Neo, a Canadian food safety technology company, is pitching Indian exporters on its unique method to pasteurize and process dry goods like seeds, nuts and herbs for export to countries with strict food safety regulations.
India, the world's No. 1 spice exporter, is a potentially huge market for the technology, says Shivam Chandran, senior global sales manager at Agri-Neo and part of the Canadian trade mission.

"A lot of the customers we’ve spoken to say that the [Indian] domestic market is also changing considerably, so in the next two to three years they’re going to be looking for better food safety technologies," said Chandran.
Seed and nut vendors are seen in Crawford Market in Mumbai, India. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

Paola Duncan, CEO of OrionSea Enterprises, a Canadian exporter of pulses, says that India opened a new tender last week for 60,000 tonnes of lentils, after a bad crop in India this year increased demand.
Canada is already a top supplier, but "needs to be more competitive price-wise and quality-wise in order to stay in the market," Duncan said.
Aiming for $70B in 2-way trade
Finding trade opportunities is one thing but competing at scale in India is another, says Sidhu.
"We need to engage [Canadian] businesses, and we need to support businesses to come to markets like India," he said. "It's not an easy place that you can just come [to] and make a phone call."
Minister Sidhu says India wants a lot of what Canada produces
At a packed Canada-India Business Council forum in Mumbai this week, panellists spoke about the momentum behind both the trade mission and the CEPA negotiations.
Two-way trade between the countries adds up to about $30 billion annually, and the Carney government is pushing to hit $70 billion per year by 2030.

Paola Duncan, CEO of Canadian exporter OrionSea Enterprises Inc., is looking to expand pulses exports to India. 'It’s a strong market for Canada,' she said while touring the Crawford Market in southern Mumbai. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"We feel there's a brotherhood or sisterhood between the two nations. I think the political friction is over, for whatever it was," said Zia Modi, a corporate lawyer with AZB and Partners in India.

"Canadians have invested for so long in India, especially the pension funds, that they've become what I call 'Indianized,'" she said, referring to the more than $100 billion in investments and portfolio holdings in 2025, according to Export Development Canada.
"They know our culture, they know the flavour, they've become very thoughtful and intelligent about where they want to invest, why they want to invest and with whom they want to invest."
Modi says geopolitical tensions, particularly with the U.S., and timing are a large part of the push for more bilateral trade.
"Canada has to become more self-reliant, and we have to become self-reliant," she said. "New partnerships will be forged, for sure."
Canada races to secure free-trade agreement with India by year-end

articles.title: Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with her third child: 'This one releases in December'
articles.summary: Actress Hilary Swank, 52, has announced she's pregnant with her third child. It's the latest example of a growing trend in Canada and the U.S. of people choosing to have children later in life.

image.caption: Hilary Swank has announced she's expecting her third child, with the 52-year-old hinting on Instagram that the due date is in December. (Charles Sykes/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Actress Hilary Swank, 52, has announced she's pregnant with her third child. It's the latest example of a growing trend in Canada and the U.S. of people choosing to have children later in life.
The star previously gave birth to twins in 2023 at the age of 48
Hilary Swank may be 52, but it's not slowing down her family — the Yellowjackets star has announced she's pregnant with her third child.
The two-time Oscar winner is already mom to two children with her husband, Philip Schneider. After freezing her eggs at age 37, she welcomed twins Aya and Ohm in 2023 when she was 48.

Swank dropped the news on Wednesday with a light-hearted Instagram video showing her family dancing in a dark room with glow sticks on their bodies to make them look like stick figures. In the video, Swank turns around to reveal a tiny glow-stick-figure in a circle on her belly.

"A lot of people have been asking what project I'm doing next," she wrote in the caption. "This one releases in December," she added, with an emoji of a baby angel, suggesting this is when the baby is due.

Swank has previously spoken about how happy she is to have waited to have children, telling Women's Health in 2025 that she feels she's a different parent than she would've been even in her early 40s.

"I'm much more patient. I'm much more understanding," she said. "And I have my career that's already established, so I'm not divided. I'm able to really sink in and be present with them and be a hands-on parent."

The American actress won her first Oscar at 25 years old with her starring role in the 2000 film Boys Don't Cry, following it up with a second best actress Oscar for the 2004 film Million Dollar Baby. Most recently, she appeared in the Netflix series Away and Showtime's Yellowjackets.
She's also spent the past few years lobbying the California government to pass bills requiring manufacturers to disclose ingredients in diapers and in prenatal vitamins.

Swank isn't the first celebrity to welcome kids in her 50s. Pop icon Janet Jackson and supermodel Naomi Campbell both had children at age 50, in 2017 and 2021 respectively, with Campbell welcoming a second child at age 53. Brigitte Nielsen, of Beverly Hills Cop II fame, gave birth to her fifth child and only daughter in 2018 at the age of 54.
Late pregnancies a growing trend
Advanced maternal age pregnancies — defined as occurring past the age of 35 — are becoming more common in North America.

In 2021, a quarter of mothers were 35 or older when they gave birth, compared with just 16 per cent 20 years earlier, according to Statistics Canada. In the U.S., federal data shows 21 per cent of births in 2023 were to those aged 35 or older, up from nine per cent in 1990.

items: After years of calls for data, study confirms Black Canadians face higher risk of maternal complications
6 moments from the untold history of childbirth
Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?

blocks.text: Natural pregnancy is possible at any time before menopause, but the chances go down as you age.
Anne Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child, telling Access Hollywood in July she was "overjoyed" that it had happened.
"When you get to a certain age, that hope looks like it's about one per cent to two per cent," she said. "It's a blessing that we do not take for granted."
Anne Hathaway, 43, seen on the red carpet last month in New York City, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)
The majority of later-stage pregnancies like Swank's are possible through modern technology such as egg-freezing or in vitro fertilization (IVF), which can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Egg-freezing allows families to press pause by extracting and preserving eggs from the ovaries at a younger age, before the eggs degrade in number and quality, which happens naturally with aging. The eggs can be stored at fertility clinics for decades, if desired, before being reimplanted when a person decides they're ready to try to conceive a child.
Developments in medical care have made pregnancy and birth safer over the years, but medical experts caution that the risk of complications with pregnancy still increases at an advanced maternal age.

And although egg-freezing is growing in popularity in Canada, providing more options for when to start a family, the procedures averaged $12,000 to $15,000 in 2024 — not quite accessible for every Canadian.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led coalition forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden
articles.summary:
Witnesses report at least six explosions near palace used by Yemen's internationally recognized government

At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by

blocks.text: At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the port city of Aden, witnesses said.

An official told the Associated Press that at least two people were killed, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility. Government military sources in Yemen told Agence-France Press (AFP) that at least four people were killed and 10 wounded.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Yemeni prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”.

It was a rare attack on the palace area, as fighting has escalated between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition on the latest front in the Iran war. The explosions caused panic among residents, who fled the area.

At least two people were killed and six wounded, said the official, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The government said the Houthis attacked with missiles and drones, the Aden-based Saba news agency reported.
A security official told the AP that at least two explosions were on top of the hill near Al-Maashiq palace, and two others were near the security gate.

AFP also reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity on Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command center for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command center was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report that the prime minister was in the presidential palace at the time of Houthi attack. Many of Yemen’s government leaders are living in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official told the AP.

The Houthis said they attacked a military operations headquarters with the “Saudi enemy”, part of their strategy of attacking Saudi targets that has included a series of attacks on airports and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom.

The escalation has complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted.

Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport.

The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase.
Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said the headquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks, and reported damage to the building.

Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.

articles.title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US election offices
articles.summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.

blocks.text: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman said.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

articles.title: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges
articles.summary: Maduro and his wife were charged with leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

image.caption: Nicolas Maduro and Cilia Flores' trial is set to begin in 2027Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro appeared in court on Thursday, where he rejected newly unsealed torture charges against him and his wife, Cilia Flores.
He said the indictment represented "false accusations" against him.
Maduro was combative in court as he was asked to enter a plea to the charges, condemning allegations of torture as "false accusations and false testimony."
Ultimately, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein interjected to declare that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro."
Flores told the judge through the Spanish interpreter: "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."

The court appearance was the latest for the pair, who are currently in US custody in New York City, now eight months since they were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a nighttime raid.
The new torture charges against the couple have been added to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced.
Maduro and Flores' trial is set to begin June 14, 2027, according to a schedule approved by the judge Thursday.
What are the torture charges?
Maduro and his wife have been accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans, during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.
They are said to have committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.
Security forces have been accused of torturing prisoners with electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.
Maduro stands accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims' treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner's child as a form of psychological torture.
For her part, Cilia Flores has been accused of helping develop the repressive system and ordering the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but the US indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

Maudro has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents, but the court has not served him with a warrant.
Torture is considered a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside of the nation where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims' nationality.

But in the US, the prosecution of foreign officials is exceedingly rare. The only recent cases include the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad's Syria.

articles.title: Self-replicating AI: Is your fridge a cybersecurity risk?
articles.summary: Anthropic researchers warn that AI worms could soon target connected household devices and spread from one device to another. Cyberattacks on French supermarkets illustrate just how vulnerable such…

image.caption: Reorder milk by touching a screen: Smart refrigerators can make life easier ― but they could soon become an entry point for AI-powered malwareImage: Richard Drew/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the living room, a robot vacuum cleaner moves back and forth, the lights are dimmed by voice assistants, the heating is controlled via smartphone and the TV connects to the internet to access a favorite streaming service. These are all examples of the "Internet of Things," in which connected electronic devices exchange data and communicate with one another.
According to recent market research by industry association Bitkom, about half of all households in Germany use such or similar "smart home" applications — and the figure is rising.

Now, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic has published a report warning that AI-powered malware could soon infiltrate connected household devices, copy itself to other devices and become active there.

blocks.caption: 52% of German households use devices like this robot vacuum cleanerImage: Jean-François Frey/PHOTOPQR/L'ALSACE/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Computer viruses that copy themselves from one machine to another have existed for decades. They are also known as worms and follow a predefined sequence of instructions. They exploit known security vulnerabilities or poorly protected access points. However, once the vulnerabilities are patched up or suitable attack vectors are no longer available, a worm can no longer spread so easily.

AI worms, however, would be far more complex and potentially much more harmful. They could solve problems autonomously and adapt to different devices, for example by coping with a different operating system or limited memory. They might also figure out for themselves how to operate on other devices or identify and circumvent new security updates
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?
Spreading via TVs

Anthropic researchers investigated whether AI models could also run on relatively inexpensive hardware. In an experiment, they distributed an AI model across 15 low-cost Android TV boxes, with each device handling part of the computation. This demonstrated that certain AI applications can run without a large data center.

In a controlled test environment, the researchers set up eight additional simulated Android devices. The AI model was able to infiltrate one of them, replicate itself and infect other devices. In four out of five attempts, it reached all eight target devices. In the remaining attempt, it reached seven of the eight.

If equipped with malware, such an AI model could potentially adapt relatively quickly to previously unknown environments and disrupt processes and operations. It could learn to circumvent various security measures rather than simply exploiting a single vulnerability. According to Anthropic's developers, this sort of "AI worm" could take roughly one to two days to establish itself on a new, previously unknown device.
A botnet of household devices?

One particularly worrying possibility is that AI could link the infected devices into a large botnet. A single infected device has limited computing power, but the more devices are compromised, the faster the AI worm could spread. The malware would no longer depend on a central server that could simply be shut down.
It might also continuously learn as it spreads. It is conceivable that it could jump to entirely different types of electronic devices, all running different software.

Infected devices could be disconnected from the network and security vulnerabilities could still be patched. The malware's decentralized structure, however, would make it difficult to contain. Anthropic itself compares this potential development to a digital slime mold slowly spreading.

Researchers at Anthropic deliberately made access to the test devices very easy and left out major digital safeguards. Even so, the company believes smaller AI models could reach the necessary level of capability later this year to spread in the real world.
Overheating cooling systems

The potential consequences of cyberattacks on connected control systems has already been seen in an incident in France. Overnight into Monday, attackers tampered with refrigeration and freezer systems at numerous supermarkets. Temperatures in the affected units rose to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. Food spoiled, and some incidents also involved fires and technical damage.

France's cybersecurity agency, CERT-FR, initially confirmed that remote-control systems made by Danish manufacturer Danfoss had been compromised. The warning was later extended to systems made by other manufacturers. Investigations into the circumstances of the attack are ongoing.

blocks.caption: Many perishable foods had to be discarded after the massive cyberattack on supermarkets in FranceImage: Fred Tanneau/AFP

blocks.text: Modern supermarkets use digital controllers to monitor and regulate refrigeration systems. Maintenance companies can access these systems remotely, for example to check temperatures. However, some of the security software was reportedly outdated, which the attackers may have exploited as an entry point for their cyberattack.
A new dimension in cyberattacks?

It remains unclear who was behind the attacks in France and what motivated them. There is also no evidence so far that a self-replicating AI worm was used in the attacks on French refrigeration systems. However, Anthropic's latest research shows how significantly AI could facilitate the development of malware, potentially enabling attacks on connected devices with serious consequences and without requiring much computing power.

Fearing further attacks, France's cybersecurity agency advised all companies to update their connected devices regularly, install essential security patches and, where possible, to disable unnecessary internet access altogether.
This article was originally published in German.
Will AI destroy humanity?

articles.title: Arizona university to 'part ways' with coach who oversaw training where Matthew Mayich collapsed
articles.summary: Arizona State University says it parted ways with the hockey coach who was leading the team when Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapsed during a workout in August. Mayich's family's…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

Arizona State University says it parted ways with the hockey coach who was leading the team when Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapsed during a workout in August. Mayich's family's lawyer said the 21-year-old remains in hospital in serious condition.
Arizona State University hires ex-NHL coach Dave Hakstol to replace Greg Powers

Arizona State University (ASU) says it will "part ways" with the hockey coach who oversaw the training at which Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on a hot day this August.
ASU has “reached a mutual agreement to part ways with hockey coach Greg Powers,” officials said in a statement Thursday, adding that former NHL coach Dave Hakstol will replace him.
Mayich, an NHL prospect drafted by the St. Louis Blues, remains in hospital in serious condition, his family’s lawyer, Robert Carey, said Thursday.

In an initial review released last month, ASU official James Rund wrote that Mayich collapsed at a training at ASU’s Tempe campus just before 8:30 a.m. Aug. 20. The review also said coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

items: Family of Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich says new university review into his collapse falls short

blocks.text: ASU then said it would commission an independent review, to be conducted by former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales.

Mayich's family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances around the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to his collapse. Mayich's parents say he was healthy prior to the workout. The family's lawyers said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.
Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout
Family says Powers should cooperate with investigation

"Our focus remains where it has been since August 20, on Matthew, and making sure what happened to him is fully understood and never happens to another player," the Mayich family said in a statement through Carey Thursday.

They said Bales's investigation must continue "with its full scope, gathering all digital evidence and covering everyone involved in that morning’s workout and in approving it, and its findings must be made public."

"Coach Powers’s departure should not limit his cooperation or anyone else’s, and the players who have spoken up must be protected," the family added. "We wish Coach Hakstol, his staff, and the players a safe and successful season."

items: Arizona university hockey coach put on paid leave after report on Canadian player Matthew Mayich's collapse

blocks.text: Seven of Mayich's teammates anonymously sent a letter to ASU's president Michael Crow on Sept. 28, disputing some findings from the school's review of the workout that led to his collapse. Players alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

It urged that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."

Powers had been ASU’s head coach since 2015 and, in 2022, signed a five-year contract extension through the 2026-27 season. He was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 30, ASU said in a statement. ASU assistant coach Mike Corbett was appointed to lead the team.
University hires Colorado Avalanche assistant coach

Before ASU announced hiring Hakstol on Thursday, he had been working as an assistant coach for the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche. He previously worked as a head coach with the Philadelphia Flyers and the Seattle Kraken, as well as an assistant for the Toronto Maple Leafs.

ASU Athletics Director Graham Rossini also announced that former NHL player Matt Greene, who played for the Los Angeles Kings and Edmonton Oilers, would join the team as an assistant along with current assistant, Jimmy Mullin. Corbett’s status was not announced.
Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

articles.title: An Australian band’s ‘unreal’ journey to break a gig world record
articles.summary: The dream rock band called Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia by car, helicopter and plane to play nine shows in 12 hours.

blocks.text: Dream rock band Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia to play nine shows, setting a new Guinness World Record for most concerts performed in 12 hours across multiple cities.
In order to beat the record, venues needed to be at least 50km apart in cities populated by more than 15,000 people, with half of the cities needing to have populations of at least 100,000.
Fathom partnered with a mental health service, Beyond Blue, donating half of the revenue from ticket sales and merchandise.
The BBC sat down with the duo to recount the day full of excitement and hurdles.

articles.title: Eels keep dying in hydro dam turbines. A new design could change that
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we learn how hydro dam turbines kill migrating eels and check out technology that could save them, see how a heat pump works and find out why an airship…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, I'm Alexandra. When we came across this story about eels dying in droves at hydro dams, our first thought was: if this was birds and windmills, there'd be an uproar. Our slippery friends deserve to navigate their waterways safely. Here's a company that's working on a tech solution to this problem.
This week:

items: Eels keep dying in hydro dam turbines. A new design could change that
The Big Picture: How a heat pump works
Why an airship was spotted hovering over this central Alberta town

blocks.text: Eels keep dying in hydro dam turbines. A new design could change that

American eels have to pass through the blades of hydropower plant turbines as they migrate down the St. Lawrence River, a perilous journey that has only a 74 per cent survival rate at one power plant. New turbine runners could change that, Natal Energy says. (Stephany Hildebrand)
Every year, thousands of endangered American eels swim down the St. Lawrence River on their way to their breeding grounds in the Sargasso Sea in the Caribbean.
But many of them are struck and killed by the turbine blades of the hydroelectric dams spanning the river, one factor contributing to a 99 per cent population decline in the area since the 1970s.

Researchers at Natel Energy, a California startup specializing in fish-friendly turbines, say they’ve designed a turbine runner that would stop those fatalities — without sacrificing power generation efficiency.

“For many decades, people thought that if you were going to protect fish, you're going to lose power, or you're going to incur some large civil work expenditure,” Kate Stirr, Natal Energy's vice-president of external affairs, told CBC News.
“What's illustrated by [our] study is that there's no trade-off between power generation and fish survival that's necessary to make.”
Why declining eels are a big deal

American eels are Canada’s only true catadromous species, meaning they’re born in the ocean, then swim upstream to spend their adult lives in freshwater locations like Lake Ontario, sometimes for up to 20 years. Finally, after growing sometimes over a metre in length, they swim back out to the ocean to spawn.

Seen as a key indicator of the biodiversity of the region, the eel has also long been important and even sacred to Indigenous people along Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers. And although they’ve historically been abundant in Lake Ontario, their numbers have plummeted due to overfishing, habitat loss and hydroelectric dams. By the late 2010s, just 18,000 passed through fish ladders at the Moses-Saunders Power Dam each year on average, down from a million in the '80s. As all of the American eels in the St. Lawrence River basin are breeding females, their migration downstream is important for the success of the overall species.

Commercial fishing of eels was banned in Ontario in 2004, and various programs have attempted to combat population drops, such as one funded by Ontario Power Generation paying fishermen to trap live eels and transfer them down the river to bypass hydro plants.

Testing in the late '90s found that more than a third of the eels trying to migrate downstream were killed by hydroelectric dams on the St. Lawrence River, with turbines at the Moses-Saunders Dam alone killing roughly 26 per cent of the eels that passed through.
The dam provides power to both the U.S. and Ontario, and is one of two mainstem hydroelectric plants on the St. Lawrence that eels must survive to reach the ocean.
A less deadly turbine

Natel's new “FishSafe” turbine design features a more curved blade shape and a “thick, blunt leading edge” instead of a thin one, providing a more glancing blow that reduces the chance of injury if a fish is struck by the rotating blades. It also minimizes the gap between the blade and its housing to lower the chance of fish getting trapped.
A computer simulation of turbines on the U.S. side of the Moses-Saunders dam found the new design could raise the survival rate of American eels passing through to 98 per cent.
The eels in the St. Lawrence River basin are overwhelmingly breeding females, making their survival important to the overall species (Stephany Hildebrand)
The new blade design also demonstrated a comparable efficiency as existing ones, and can be installed without costly full-system overhauls in most cases.

“If we can have a solution where the runner just is an in-place upgrade, then it makes it very easy for the owner to think about a solution that protects fish in addition to modernizing their plant,” Stirr said.

A lot of the existing hydropower plants in North America and in Europe are decades old, she said. Natel Energy is hoping that its new proof-of-concept will show hydro dam companies that prioritizing fish survival won’t cut into their bottom line, and convince more to come on board.
A rendering of one of Natel Energy’s FishSafe turbines. (Natel Energy)

She said the firm has been in conversation with Canadian companies, and recently installed some of its turbine runners at a plant in France that was subject to regulations protecting European eels. The turbines have since been successfully tested with live eels.
“We love eels, and I would say that this technology, we hope, can really be a game-changer for the American eel population.”
—Alexandra Mae Jones

Reader feedback
Last week's issue included a story on why Fredericton Botanic Garden planted three ash trees upside down. The trees were among 14 removed after they were infected with emerald ash borer.

Gord Campbell wrote: "You failed to mention that there is a vaccine that can protect an ash tree for up to three years per injection, costing between $150 and $350 per tree. We have had excellent success protecting our beautiful ash for about the last 15 years. The cost of removing a dead or dying ash tree often exceeds preventive treatment."

The City of Fredericton is trying to slow the emerald ash borer beetles down with the vaccine-like insecticide TreeAzin and with pheromone traps to catch the adult beetles. But there has been debate in some cities about whether it's better to vaccinate trees, which some say is just "delaying the inevitable," or spend the same money on cutting and replacing them.

Lena Measures wrote in about balcony solar panels: "These inexpensive, easy-to-install plug-in solar panels are having a moment in Germany and starting to sell in other places such as the U.S. Some are sold at Ikea. Are they a good idea and why are they not available in Canada?"
